title: Assessing Markov Persistence Beyond Seasonality in Monthly Rainfall-State Prediction in Chad
content: Does the previous month’s rainfall state improve forecasts once the calendar month is known? We used monthly rainfall records from Chad’s national meteorological agency (ANAM) for 2010–2020. The records cover 60 stations and 7,107 of 7,920 possible station-months. We analyzed four historical stations and extended the comparison to 30 stations selected for completeness, including the original four. An event was a monthly accumulation ≥ 20 mm. We compared calendar-month frequencies, homogeneous and two-season Markov chains, and seasonal logistic regressions with and without the previous state. Across 1,735 eligible rolling-origin forecasts in 2016–2020, pooled Brier scores were 0.05755 for calendar-month climatology, 0.07918 for the two-season Markov chain and 0.05789 for harmonic regression with a lag. The two-season chain outperformed climatology at one station. Adding the lag could improve a given seasonal regression, but the comparison yielded no consistent advantage over climatology. Seventeen discrepancies in annual summaries concern fields excluded from the models. Monthly measurements await independent verification, and missing rainy-season observations affect forecast eligibility. Retrospective station selection and sensitivity to the seasonal model limit generalization.
